title: Reading the Psalms

objectives.can: Read a short psalm, recognising its common vocabulary and its movement from address to petition to praise.
Recognise twelve words characteristic of the Psalms.

explanation.summary: A psalm is a prayer or song addressed to God, and many of them follow a path: a call on God, a complaint or need, a petition, and a turn to trust and praise. Psalm 13 shows the path in six verses. This lesson also gives you twelve words that fill the Psalms, each with a range of sense and not one English word.

sections.heading: The path of a psalm of lament
body: Many psalms begin by speaking to God, set out a trouble, ask for help, and end in trust or praise. Psalm 13 has the whole path. Verses 2 and 3 are complaint, four times עַד אָנָה, 'how long?'. Verse 4 is petition, with three imperatives: הַבִּיטָה, עֲנֵנִי and הָאִירָה, 'look, answer me, light up'. Verse 5 gives the reasons for the petition: the clauses with פֶּן, 'lest', say what the poet fears. Verse 6 turns: וַאֲנִי, 'but as for me', and then trust, בָטַחְתִּי, and a vow to sing, אָשִׁירָה.

This is a common pattern and not a rule. Scholars since Hermann Gunkel have sorted the Psalms into types such as laments, hymns and thanksgivings, and they note that psalms often mix the parts or leave some out. Read the psalm in front of you, and use the pattern only to ask where you are in it.

sections.heading: The 'how long?' and the turn
body: עַד אָנָה, 'how long?', is not a request for information. It is the voice of complaint, and it is spoken to God. In 13:2 it is paired with two verbs, תִּשְׁכָּחֵנִי and תַּסְתִּיר, 'will you forget me, will you hide'; in 13:3 it is paired with two more, אָשִׁית and יָרוּם. Four 'how long' clauses in two verses give the complaint its weight.

The turn comes with a small word. At the start of 13:6, וַאֲנִי puts the speaker in contrast with the enemies of verse 5. The verb בָטַחְתִּי is a qatal: it states the trust as something the speaker has done and still does. The cohortative אָשִׁירָה, 'let me sing', is the usual form of a vow or resolve to praise. The last clause begins with כִּי and gives the ground of the praise; how to put its qatal verb in English (has dealt, will have dealt) is a question about the sense, and translators differ.

sections.heading: Twelve words and their range of sense
body: The words of the Psalms are common words with a wide range. Do not fix one English word to each. A good reader asks which part of the range suits the verse in front of them.
The table gives the headwords of the vocabulary list. Where a verb's range depends on the stem, the stem is named.

head: Word
Range of sense
A verse to read
rows: Loyal love, kindness that keeps a bond, faithfulness; from God to people and between people
Praise; a song of praise; the deed or the one that is praised
What is right: rightness, justice, righteousness
A judging, a verdict, justice; a rule or ordinance
Life, self, a person; the throat, the appetite; the inner being
Heart, mind, will; the seat of thought as well as of feeling
Strength, might, a refuge of strength
Rock, cliff; a name for God as a place of safety
In the Piel, to praise; also to boast
In the Hiphil, to give thanks, to confess, to praise; in other stems, to throw

sections.heading: Headings and סֶלָה
body: Most psalms have a heading, and in the edition the heading is part of verse 1. Psalm 13:1 reads לַמְנַצֵּחַ מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד. The words give a title (a מִזְמוֹר is a song), a person (לְדָוִד might mean 'by', 'for' or 'belonging to David'), and a word, לַמְנַצֵּחַ, which is usually taken as an instruction to a leader or choirmaster. The exact sense of each is debated, so read the headings as old information about the use or the tradition of the psalm and not as a key to its meaning.

The word סֶלָה stands at the end of lines in many psalms and in Habakkuk 3. Its meaning is not known. It is usually taken to be a musical or liturgical direction, and the old translators guessed at it. A reader can note where it stands and read on.

sections.heading: Acrostic psalms
body: Some poems are built as acrostics: each verse or line begins with the next letter of the alphabet. Psalm 145 is one. Verse 2 begins בְּכָל, verse 3 begins גָּדוֹל and verse 4 begins דּוֹר, the letters bet, gimel and dalet. Verse 1 begins with the heading, and its first word of poetry is אֲרוֹמִמְךָ, with aleph. In the Masoretic Text the verse for nun is missing between verses 13 and 14. Psalm 119 gives eight verses to each letter, and the first three verses of Lamentations 1 begin with the first three letters (אֵיכָה, בָּכוֹ, גָּלְתָה) in turn.

misunderstandings: A lament is not a lack of faith. The 'how long?' questions are spoken to God and are part of the prayer.
One English word cannot stand for each Hebrew word. נֶפֶשׁ is not always 'soul', and חֶסֶד is not always 'mercy'. Read the range and choose with the verse.
The heading of a psalm is not the first line of its poetry. In the edition the heading is verse 1, so the poem may begin at verse 2.
סֶלָה does not have a known meaning. 'Pause' or 'lift up' are guesses.

deeper.heading: Types of psalm
body: Hermann Gunkel's early twentieth-century classification of the Psalms by type has shaped nearly all later study. It rests on the observation that psalms of one type share a pattern of parts, which is why a complaint, a petition and a vow of praise turn up together in Psalm 13. Later scholars have refined the types and questioned how fixed they were, so the list of types is a map and not the ground.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: How long, O LORD, wilt Thou forget me for ever? How long wilt Thou hide Thy face from me?
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Address and complaint. יְהוָה is called on by name, and עַד אָנָה, 'how long?', is repeated. The two verbs, תִּשְׁכָּחֵנִי and תַּסְתִּיר אֶת פָּנֶיךָ מִמֶּנִּי, are parallel: 'will you forget me for ever, will you hide your face from me?'.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Behold Thou, and answer me, O LORD my God; lighten mine eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Petition. The three imperatives הַבִּיטָה, עֲנֵנִי and הָאִירָה carry the request, and אֱלֹהָי, 'my God', is the personal address. The ending -ָה on two of the imperatives is often thought to add urgency. The poet asks to be seen, answered and given light.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: But as for me, in Thy mercy do I trust; my heart shall rejoice in Thy salvation. I will sing unto the LORD, because He hath dealt bountifully with me.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The turn to trust and praise. וַאֲנִי sets the speaker against the enemies, בְּחַסְדְּךָ names the ground of the trust, and בִּישׁוּעָתֶךָ is the cause of the heart's joy. אָשִׁירָה is the cohortative of the vow to sing. The final clause begins with כִּי, 'for', and gives the reason.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Great is the LORD, and highly to be praised; and His greatness is unsearchable.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: This verse begins with גָּדוֹל, the letter gimel, in an acrostic whose verses 2 and 4 begin with bet and dalet. The word וּמְהֻלָּל is a participle of הָלַל in the Pual: 'and much praised'. The Piel sense 'to praise' is the usual one; the passive participle gives 'one who is praised'.

quoted.title: Psalms
quoted.english: Many there are that say of my soul: 'There is no salvation for him in God.' Selah
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Here the verse ends with סֶלָה after the enemies' speech, 'there is no salvation for him in God'. The word is not part of the sentence. Its meaning is unknown, and a reader can treat it as a mark in the text.

reading.why: Six short verses that run through the whole path of a lament: the heading (13:1), the address and the 'how long?' complaint (13:2–3), the petition with its imperatives (13:4), the reasons introduced by פֶּן (13:5), and the turn to trust and a vow of praise (13:6). The words חֶסֶד, יְשׁוּעָה, נֶפֶשׁ and לֵב of the vocabulary list stand in it.
